Pick B: a bio-data consequence test of the lone certified positive. The math-to-bio structural-invariant side is now effectively closed under the constraints you stated. Starting a new structural pairing now risks re-entering the same trap: finding grammar-equivalent count recurrences or visually appealing fold analogies with no forcing. The highest-leverage move is to ask whether the only surviving structural fact, near-maximal Hamming-1 synonymous edge hiding, buys a measurable biological robustness advantage.
The cleanest first experiment is:
DMS-weighted mistranslation robustness of the standard genetic code.
Use ProteinGym as the primary public dataset. It is realistically fetchable: the official ProteinGym repository describes a substitution benchmark with roughly 2.7 million missense variants across 217 DMS assays, with processed files containing mutant, mutated_sequence, DMS_score, and binarized fitness columns; higher DMS_score is consistently higher fitness across assays. GitHub
The experiment should not test codon usage. It should test the genetic code map itself.
First construct a DMS-derived amino-acid damage matrix:

$$D(a\to b)=\operatorname{median}_{\text{assays},\,\text{sites with WT }a}
\left[
S_{\mathrm{WT}}-S_{a\to b}
\right],$$

where  $S$  is the normalized DMS score within each assay. Use only single amino-acid substitutions. Winsorize or rank-normalize scores within assay so one high-dynamic-range assay cannot dominate. If a pair  $a\to b$  is poorly covered, mark it missing and either drop all code-neighbor terms needing it or use a pre-registered shrinkage estimate toward the amino-acid-pair median. Do not use amino-acid physicochemical properties.
Then evaluate a genetic code  $g:64\to 20+\mathrm{Stop}$  by its expected one-step translation-error damage:

$$R(g)=
\frac{
\sum_{c\in \mathrm{sense}}
\sum_{c'\sim c}
w(c\to c')\,
L_g(c,c')
}{
\sum_{c\in \mathrm{sense}}
\sum_{c'\sim c}
w(c\to c')
},$$

where  $c'\sim c$  means Hamming-1 codon neighbor. For a neighbor that maps to the same amino acid, set

$$L_g(c,c')=0.$$

For a missense neighbor,

$$L_g(c,c')=D(g(c)\to g(c')).$$

For a stop neighbor, use a pre-registered large penalty estimated from nonsense DMS variants if available in the same assays, otherwise run the primary analysis on sense-to-sense neighbors only and report stop-neighbor robustness separately. The primary statistic should be sense-to-sense to avoid letting Stop dominate the answer.
Use two versions of  $w(c\to c')$ .
The primary version is label-free uniform one-step error weight:

$$w=1.$$

The secondary version uses a fixed empirical mutation/misread weight by position and transition/transversion class, but this must be sensitivity analysis, not the primary result. Otherwise the test becomes about a chosen error model rather than about the graph fact.
The key statistic is:

$$T_{\mathrm{std}}=R(g_{\mathrm{std}}).$$

The pre-registered null is:

$$\Omega_{\mathrm{deg}}=
\text{all random genetic codes with the standard amino-acid/Stop degeneracy profile fixed}.$$

That means Leu, Ser, and Arg each receive six codons; the five fourfold amino acids receive four codons; Ile receives three; the nine twofold amino acids receive two; Met and Trp receive one; Stop receives three. Amino-acid labels are fixed because the DMS matrix is label-specific. Codon assignments are randomized uniformly subject to those multiplicities. Use exact enumeration only if feasible; otherwise use a fixed-seed Monte Carlo sample large enough that the tail resolution is meaningful, for example  $10^6$  to  $10^7$  codes.
Compute:

$$p_{\mathrm{robust}}=
\Pr_{\Omega_{\mathrm{deg}}}
\left[
R(g)\le R(g_{\mathrm{std}})
\right].$$

That asks: does the standard code produce less DMS-measured damage from one-step mistranslation than degeneracy-matched codes?
But the decisive part is not that p-value alone. The crucial decomposition is:

$$R(g)=
\alpha-\beta\, e_{\mathrm{in}}(g)+\epsilon_g,$$

estimated across the same null ensemble. Here  $e_{\mathrm{in}}$  is the number of Hamming-1 synonymous edges. If the certified edge-hiding extremality has biological consequence, then  $\beta>0$ : more hidden edges should lower DMS-weighted mistranslation damage.
Then run the conditioned null:

$$\Omega_{\mathrm{deg},e}=
\{g\in\Omega_{\mathrm{deg}}: e_{\mathrm{in}}(g)=e_{\mathrm{in}}(g_{\mathrm{std}})\}.$$

Compute:

$$p_{\mathrm{resid}}=
\Pr_{\Omega_{\mathrm{deg},e}}
\left[
R(g)\le R(g_{\mathrm{std}})
\right].$$

The desired outcome is not necessarily that  $p_{\mathrm{resid}}$  is tiny. In fact, the cleanest support for the current theory would be:


 $R(g_{\mathrm{std}})$  is low under  $\Omega_{\mathrm{deg}}$ .


 $e_{\mathrm{in}}$  strongly predicts low  $R(g)$  across  $\Omega_{\mathrm{deg}}$ .


The standard code is not strongly exceptional under  $\Omega_{\mathrm{deg},e}$ .


That would say: the biological robustness advantage is carried mainly by edge hiding, not by some additional hidden invariant. That is exactly aligned with the closure result.
The decisive confounders are these.
First, amino-acid property optimization. The standard code may reduce damage because neighboring codons map to chemically similar amino acids, not because edges are synonymous. The e-conditioned null addresses this. If the standard code is still extreme after fixing  $e_{\mathrm{in}}$ , the signal is not only edge hiding.
Second, DMS assay bias. ProteinGym assays differ in organism, protein class, readout, dynamic range, and selection regime. The damage matrix must be assay-normalized and then tested by leave-one-protein-family and leave-one-assay-type splits. ProteinGym explicitly aggregates benchmark metrics by UniProt ID to avoid bias from proteins with multiple assays; the same principle should be used here. GitHub
Third, expression relevance. DMS measures variant functional cost, not actual mistranslation frequency. That is acceptable for the first experiment because the question is whether hidden edges reduce potential wrong-product damage. Expression enters only as biological motivation: selection against mistranslation-induced misfolding is expected to be stronger for highly expressed proteins, a hypothesis previously argued from yeast expression/protein abundance and evolutionary-rate data. arXiv Do not overclaim that DMS directly measures expression-level selection.
Fourth, stop handling. Stop penalties can overwhelm the statistic. The primary analysis should be sense-to-sense only; Stop-inclusive robustness should be a separate sensitivity analysis.
Fifth, error-model arbitrariness. A heavily tuned mistranslation matrix can manufacture significance. The primary test must use uniform Hamming-1 weights. Empirical misread weights may be reported only as robustness checks.
This experiment is non-vacuous because it can fail in informative ways. It fails the edge-hiding consequence claim if  $e_{\mathrm{in}}$  does not predict lower DMS-weighted damage across degeneracy-matched codes, or if the standard code’s low damage is entirely residual after conditioning on  $e_{\mathrm{in}}$ . It also fails if results depend on one assay class, one protein family, or Stop penalties.
If it passes in the clean pattern above, the program gets a strong biological interpretation without reopening the closed structural-invariant search: the standard code’s certified edge-hiding extremality is not just graph-theoretic tolerance; it predicts lower experimentally measured cost of one-step mistranslation.
Sharpest next question: After conditioning on  $e_{\mathrm{in}}$ , is there any residual DMS-weighted robustness signal left in the standard code, or is the entire measurable advantage exhausted by synonymous edge hiding?**
